A coastline where new sea laps at red sand, thin foam hissing over iron-red grains, a dark green line of algae already staining the tideline rocks, the land behind still pale and dead and dry.

Dome clusters glow amber in the dusk, their interiors lush, while outside the glass the raw plain stretches red and empty in every direction, the living world pressed tight against its transparent boundary.

The first rain falls on stone that has never known it — dark wet patches spreading across a cliff face, water running in thin silver threads down bare rock, pooling in hollows where nothing yet grows.
A crater rim catches windblown seeds and moisture, its inner bowl already hazed with low green growth while the outer slopes stay barren, the crater holding its small biosphere like a cupped hand.

Glaciers of imported ice retreat under a warming sky, leaving raw wet rock and meltwater pools behind them, the exposed ground at the glacier's edge already showing the first faint green stain of pioneer algae.

A mountain range split down its spine — the windward side catching moisture and greening rapidly in streaks and patches, the leeward side still red and dry, two worlds divided by a single ridge of stone.
Broad salt flats at the edge of a new inland sea show concentric rings of life — dark algae at the water's rim, pale crust beyond, and bare cracked earth further out, each ring a year of advance.

The sky itself marks the transition — directly above the greening lowlands a thickening blue haze, but toward the barren uplands the sky fades back to thin pink, the atmospheric boundary visible as weather and color.

A single ancient canyon threads green along its floor where water collects and shelter deepens the warmth, the walls above rising sheer and lifeless to a barren plateau stretching red to every horizon.

Spidery irrigation channels radiate from a central station across a flat plain, each channel edged with a thin green line of growth, the geometry of life laid over the geometry of dead rock in straight lines.

A high plateau edge drops into a transformed lowland — standing at the rim you see red stone at your feet and a green world spreading below, the two elevations separated by a cliff and a thousand years.
Fog rolls in off the new sea each morning and retreats by midday, leaving a dark wet tidemark on the coastal rock, and in that narrow band of moisture the first mosses grip and hold and spread.

Grassland burns for the first time — a thin line of orange fire crossing a green plain, smoke rising into a still-thin sky, the burnt ground behind it black and raw, the unburnt ground ahead still vividly green.

A dry riverbed waits — upstream a dam holds back the first reservoir, its shores already greening, but downstream the old channel remains dust-grey and dead, waiting for the moment the gates open and the water comes.

Seen from orbit at the transition year, the planet is a mosaic — green smears over the lowlands, red dominates the heights, white cloud beginning to form over the warmer greened regions, the planet visibly alive and unfinished.
